categoryBlurb: The Sunday-afternoon side of Italian cooking — golden cutlets, slow braises, risotto stirred with a glass of wine in your other hand, and dough that fills the whole apartment with the smell of a good bakery.

recipes.title: Crispy Chicken Parmesan
recipes.blurb: Thin cutlets fried until they shatter, a bright five-ingredient tomato sauce, and just enough mozzarella to melt into ropes. The trick is sauce and cheese only on top, so the crust never goes soggy.

items: 2 large boneless skinless chicken breasts (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
2 cups (480 ml) neutral oil, such as canola or grapeseed, for frying
1 can (28 oz / 794 g) whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes, crushed by hand
8 oz (225 g) low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella, coarsely shredded
1/4 cup (10 g) fresh basil leaves, torn

instructions.title: Make the sauce first
instructions.text: Warm the 2 tbsp olive oil and sliced garlic in a saucepan over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet but has no brown edges. Add the hand-crushed tomatoes, 3/4 tsp salt, and the red pepper flakes, then simmer uncovered over medium-low for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then. It is ready when a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a track that fills in slowly. Stir in the basil leaves off the heat and set aside; making the sauce first means it is done before the fried cutlets have a chance to get cold.

instructions.title: Cut the breasts into cutlets
instructions.text: Lay a chicken breast flat and press one palm on top, then run a sharp knife horizontally through the middle to split it into two thin pieces. Repeat with the second breast so you have 4 cutlets. Thin cutlets cook through in the same few minutes it takes the crust to brown, which is the entire secret to chicken parm that is not dry in the middle.

instructions.title: Pound them even
instructions.text: Put each cutlet between two sheets of plastic wrap or in a zip-top bag and pound with a flat meat mallet, a small skillet, or a rolling pin until it is an even 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Work from the center outward with firm taps rather than hard smacks, which tear the meat. Even thickness matters more than thinness — a cutlet that is thin at one end and fat at the other will always overcook somewhere. Season both sides with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper.

instructions.title: Set up three stations
instructions.text: Line up three shallow dishes: flour in the first, the 3 eggs beaten with 1 tbsp water in the second, and the panko tossed with the 1/2 cup grated Parmigiano and 1 tsp oregano in the third. Keep one hand for dry and one hand for wet so your fingers do not turn into breaded clubs. Putting cheese directly into the crumbs means the crust itself tastes like Parmesan, not just the topping.

instructions.title: Bread the cutlets
instructions.text: Dredge a cutlet in flour and shake off every loose speck, dip it in egg and let the excess run off for 3 seconds, then press it firmly into the panko on both sides. Real pressure here is what makes the crust stick instead of sliding off in the pan. Set the breaded cutlets on a rack and let them rest 10 minutes if you have the time, which lets the coating hydrate and glue itself on.

instructions.title: Heat the oil correctly
instructions.text: Pour the 2 cups oil into a 12 in (30 cm) skillet — a pan that wide genuinely needs that much to sit 1/4 in (6 mm) deep — and heat over medium-high to 350°F (175°C). Without a thermometer, drop in a pinch of panko: it should sizzle steadily and float, not sit still and not crackle violently. Oil that is too cool soaks in and goes greasy; oil that is smoking burns the crumbs before the chicken is done. Let the oil cool completely before you strain it back into a jar; it is good for one or two more fries.

instructions.title: Fry two at a time
instructions.text: Lay 2 cutlets in the oil away from you and fry 3 to 4 minutes on the first side, until the edges you can see are deep golden. Flip once with tongs and fry 2 to 3 minutes more. Do not crowd the pan; four at once drops the oil temperature and you get pale, oily breading. Move the finished cutlets to a wire rack, never paper towels, so the underside stays crisp while the second batch fries.

instructions.title: Check the temperature
instructions.text: Slide an instant-read thermometer sideways into the thickest part of a cutlet — it must read 165°F (74°C) before the chicken is safe to eat. Pounded cutlets almost always get there during the fry, but if one reads low, put it back in the oil for another minute rather than hoping the broiler will catch it. Never rely on the color of the crust to tell you the chicken is cooked; panko goes golden long before a thick spot is done, and it can also brown while the very center is still cool.

instructions.title: Sauce and cheese the tops only
instructions.text: Heat the broiler with a rack 6 in (15 cm) below the element. Arrange the cutlets on a foil-lined sheet pan, spoon about 3 tbsp of sauce onto the center of each, and leave a wide border of bare crust all the way around. Divide the shredded mozzarella and 1/4 cup Parmigiano over the sauce. Sauce touching the crust is the number one reason chicken parm turns soggy, so resist the urge to drown it.

instructions.title: Broil just until bubbling
instructions.text: Broil for 2 to 4 minutes, watching the whole time, until the mozzarella is melted with a few brown blisters. Broilers vary wildly and cheese goes from perfect to burnt in about 30 seconds, so do not walk away or check your phone. Pull the pan the moment the cheese stops looking rubbery and starts to bubble at the edges.

instructions.title: Rest, then serve
instructions.text: Let the cutlets sit for 3 minutes so the molten cheese sets enough to slice without sliding off. Scatter the torn basil over the top and serve the remaining sauce warm in a bowl on the side for dipping or for a small pile of spaghetti. Serve immediately — chicken parm is at its best about four minutes out of the broiler and never really comes back.

tips: Bread the cutlets up to 6 hours ahead and keep them on a rack in the fridge, uncovered. The coating dries slightly and fries up even crisper.
No San Marzano tomatoes? Any can of whole peeled tomatoes works better than pre-crushed, which is usually made from lower-grade fruit and tastes tinny.
Fresh mozzarella in water releases too much liquid under a broiler and floods the crust. Use the firm low-moisture block and shred it yourself.
If the breading slides off in the pan, the cutlets were wet or the flour layer was too thick. Pat them dry and tap off the flour like you mean it.
Leftovers reheat well at 375°F (190°C) on a rack for 10 minutes. The microwave will turn that crust into a wet paper towel.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken is safe and still juicy at 165°F (74°C) measured at the thickest point of the cutlet.
recipes.pairing: A simple arugula salad with lemon and a glass of Chianti Classico, with garlic bread for the extra sauce.

recipes.title: Chicken Piccata with Lemon and Capers
recipes.blurb: Golden cutlets under a sharp, buttery lemon-caper pan sauce that comes together in the same skillet in about four minutes. This is the weeknight dinner that tastes like you tried much harder than you did.

items: 2 large boneless skinless chicken breasts (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
2 tbsp (30 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, plus 1 tsp (5 ml) more for the second batch
1/2 cup (120 ml) dry white wine, such as Pinot Grigio
3 tbsp (45 ml) fresh lemon juice (about 1 1/2 lemons)
3 tbsp (27 g) capers, drained and rinsed
4 tbsp (55 g) cold unsalted butter, cut into 4 pieces
3 tbsp (12 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 lemon, cut into thin rounds, for serving

instructions.title: Split and pound the breasts
instructions.text: Press one hand flat on a chicken breast and slice it horizontally into two thin pieces, then repeat with the second breast for 4 cutlets total. Put each between plastic wrap and pound to an even 1/4 in (6 mm) with a mallet or small skillet. At that thickness the cutlets cook in about 6 minutes total, which is the whole point of piccata.

instructions.title: Season and dredge
instructions.text: Season the cutlets on both sides with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, then dredge each in the 1/2 cup flour and shake off the excess until you see only a thin, dusty film. Too much flour goes gummy in the sauce and tastes raw. Dredge right before cooking, because flour sitting on damp chicken turns into paste within a few minutes.

instructions.title: Heat the skillet
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) stainless steel skillet over medium-high heat, add the 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp butter, and wait until the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers. Skip nonstick if you can — the browned bits that stick to stainless steel are the backbone of the sauce. If the butter turns dark brown immediately, the pan is too hot; pull it off for 20 seconds.

instructions.title: Brown the first two cutlets
instructions.text: Lay 2 cutlets in the pan and cook 3 minutes without moving them, until the underside is golden and releases easily from the pan. Flip and cook 2 minutes more. They should sizzle steadily and confidently, not scream or smoke. Crowding the pan drops the heat and steams the chicken gray, so do not try to fit all four.

instructions.title: Cook the second batch
instructions.text: Move the first two cutlets to a plate and repeat with the remaining two, adding the extra 1 tsp oil if the pan looks dry. Check the thickest cutlet with an instant-read thermometer: 165°F (74°C) means done, and anything under that goes back in the pan for another minute. Tent the plate loosely with foil and let the chicken rest while you build the sauce — the juices that pool on that plate go into the sauce at the end, so do not tip them into the sink.

instructions.title: Deglaze with wine
instructions.text: Pour the 1/2 cup white wine into the hot skillet and scrape the bottom hard with a wooden spoon as it bubbles — every brown fleck is concentrated chicken flavor. Let the wine reduce over medium-high heat for about 2 minutes, until it has cooked down by half and no longer smells sharply of alcohol. This step is what separates a real pan sauce from lemon butter.

instructions.title: Build the sauce body
instructions.text: Add the 3/4 cup chicken stock, 3 tbsp lemon juice, and 3 tbsp capers, and simmer briskly for 3 to 4 minutes until the liquid reduces to about 2/3 cup and coats the back of a spoon lightly. Rinsing the capers first keeps the sauce from turning aggressively salty. Taste it now — it should be bracingly lemony, because the butter is about to soften all of that.

instructions.title: Mount the butter off the heat
instructions.text: Take the skillet completely off the burner, wait 15 seconds, then add the 4 tbsp cold butter one piece at a time, swirling the pan constantly until each piece disappears. Cold butter added off direct heat emulsifies into a glossy sauce; butter dumped into a boiling pan splits into greasy pools. The sauce should look silky and slightly thickened, like warm cream.

instructions.title: Return the chicken
instructions.text: Slide the cutlets and any juices from the plate back into the skillet and turn them once to coat, keeping the pan off the heat or on the lowest possible setting. Ninety seconds is plenty to warm them through. Boiling the chicken in the sauce now would both overcook it and break the emulsion you just made.

instructions.title: Finish and serve
instructions.text: Stir in the 3 tbsp chopped parsley, taste, and add a pinch more salt or a squeeze of lemon if it feels flat. Serve straight from the skillet or on a warm platter with the lemon rounds tucked around, spooning the sauce generously over each cutlet. Piccata sauce thickens as it cools, so get it to the table right away.

tips: No wine in the house? Use an extra 1/2 cup (120 ml) stock plus 1 extra tsp lemon juice. The sauce will be a little less complex but still excellent.
Bottled lemon juice tastes metallic here and there is nowhere to hide it. Squeeze real lemons — you need about a lemon and a half.
Veal or pork cutlets pounded to the same 1/4 in (6 mm) work identically; pork should hit 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest.
If the sauce breaks and looks oily, pull it off the heat and whisk in 1 tbsp cold stock or an ice cube to bring it back together.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken cutlets are done at 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; pull them from the pan the moment they get there.
recipes.pairing: Buttered angel hair or roasted asparagus, and the rest of the Pinot Grigio you cooked with.

recipes.title: Chicken Marsala with Mushrooms
recipes.blurb: Deeply browned mushrooms, sweet Marsala cooked down until it is almost syrupy, and cutlets that soak it all up. It is a thirty-five minute dinner that eats like a restaurant special.

items: 2 large boneless skinless chicken breasts (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
10 oz (285 g) cremini mushrooms, sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
2 medium shallots, finely chopped (about 1/2 cup / 70 g)
3 tbsp (42 g) cold unsalted butter, cut into 3 pieces
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Make even cutlets
instructions.text: Slice each breast horizontally into two thin pieces, then pound them between plastic wrap to an even 1/3 in (8 mm). You want 4 cutlets of the same thickness so they all finish at the same moment. Season both sides with the 1 1/4 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper.

instructions.title: Dredge lightly
instructions.text: Coat each cutlet in the 1/2 cup flour and tap off everything that is not clinging. The flour does two jobs: it browns fast for color, and the starch that sheds into the pan later helps thicken the Marsala sauce. A heavy, pasty coat will make the finished sauce cloudy and taste of raw flour.

instructions.title: Sear the cutlets
instructions.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) stainless skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then cook 2 cutlets at a time for 3 minutes on the first side and 2 on the second, until deeply golden. Work in two batches so the pan stays hot. Move them to a plate — they will finish cooking in the sauce, so a little pink in the very center is fine at this stage.

instructions.title: Brown the mushrooms hard
instructions.text: Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil and the 2 tbsp butter to the same pan, then add the sliced mushrooms in one layer and leave them alone for 3 full minutes. They will release water and look sad, then the water will boil off and they will start to brown. Keep cooking 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring occasionally, until they are genuinely dark brown at the edges. Undercooked, gray mushrooms are the most common thing wrong with homemade marsala.

instructions.title: Add shallots and garlic
instructions.text: Stir in the chopped shallots with a pinch of salt and cook 2 minutes until softened and translucent, then add the minced garlic and cook just 30 seconds more until fragrant. Garlic added earlier would burn against the hot mushrooms and turn bitter. The pan bottom should now be covered in brown glaze.

instructions.title: Deglaze with Marsala
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup Marsala and immediately scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon while it bubbles hard. Let it reduce over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until the liquid is thick, glossy, and reduced by about half. This is the flavor engine of the dish — rushing it leaves a raw, boozy sweetness that no amount of cream will fix.

instructions.title: Simmer with stock
instructions.text: Add the 1 cup chicken stock and 1 tsp thyme leaves and simmer over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, until the sauce reduces by roughly a third and lightly coats a spoon. Scrape the pan again as it reduces. The sauce should smell nutty and winey rather than sharp.

instructions.title: Add the cream
instructions.text: Stir in the 1/3 cup heavy cream and let it bubble gently for 2 minutes to thicken slightly and turn the sauce a soft caramel color. Traditional Marsala is often made without cream, but a small amount rounds off the sweetness of the wine beautifully. Do not let it hit a rolling boil or it can separate.

instructions.title: Return the chicken
instructions.text: Nestle the cutlets and every drop of resting juice back into the pan, spoon sauce over them, and simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes. Check the thickest cutlet with a thermometer: you are looking for 165°F (74°C). The cutlets will drink up sauce as they finish, which is exactly what you want.

instructions.title: Finish with cold butter
instructions.text: Pull the pan off the heat and swirl in the 3 tbsp cold butter, one piece at a time, until the sauce turns glossy and slightly thicker. Taste and adjust with salt and a few grinds of pepper. Scatter the 2 tbsp parsley over the top and serve immediately, with plenty of sauce spooned over each piece.

tips: Buy dry Marsala, not sweet, and never the salted cooking Marsala from the vinegar aisle. A drinkable bottle costs about ten dollars and lasts months.
Mixing in 4 oz (115 g) of sliced shiitake or rehydrated porcini with the cremini gives the sauce far more depth for almost no extra work.
Do not wash mushrooms under running water; wipe them with a damp towel so they brown instead of steaming.
The sauce can be made through the cream step a day ahead and refrigerated. Reheat gently, then sear fresh cutlets and combine.
If the sauce gets too thick while resting, loosen it with a splash of stock rather than water so you do not dilute the flavor.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken is done at 165°F (74°C); simmer it in the sauce only until it reaches that, or it will go stringy.
recipes.pairing: Creamy polenta or mashed potatoes to catch the sauce, with a glass of Barbera or the dry Marsala itself.

recipes.title: Chicken Saltimbocca alla Romana
recipes.blurb: Sage leaves pressed onto thin cutlets, wrapped in prosciutto, and crisped in butter until the ham goes crackly. The name means jump in the mouth, and after one bite you will understand why.

items: 2 large boneless skinless chicken breasts (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g total)
8 thin slices prosciutto di Parma (about 4 oz / 115 g)
2 tbsp (30 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, plus 1 tsp (5 ml) more for the second batch
3 tbsp (42 g) cold unsalted butter, cut into 3 pieces
1/4 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Make four thin cutlets
instructions.text: Slice each breast horizontally into two pieces, then pound them between plastic wrap to a very even 1/4 in (6 mm). Saltimbocca lives or dies on thinness — the prosciutto needs to crisp in the same 3 minutes the chicken takes to cook. Pat the cutlets completely dry with paper towels.

instructions.title: Season carefully
instructions.text: Season the cutlets with only the 1/2 tsp kosher salt and all of the 3/4 tsp pepper. Prosciutto is already very salty and it will season the whole dish as it cooks, so this is one of the rare times you deliberately underseason the meat. Pepper, on the other hand, you want plenty of.

instructions.title: Layer sage and prosciutto
instructions.text: Lay 3 sage leaves down the length of each cutlet, then drape 2 slices of prosciutto over the top so they overlap slightly and cover the surface almost completely. Press the prosciutto down firmly with your palm — the moisture from the chicken makes it stick without any toothpicks. Do not wrap the prosciutto all the way around; leaving the bottom bare lets that side brown properly.

instructions.title: Flour only the bare side
instructions.text: Dust the naked chicken side of each cutlet lightly with the flour and shake off the excess, leaving the prosciutto side completely bare. The floured side browns evenly, and the unfloured ham side crisps directly against the metal. Handle them gently so the sage stays put.

instructions.title: Heat the pan
instructions.text: Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat, add the 2 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter, and swirl until the butter has foamed and the foam has just started to settle. The combination gives you the browning power of oil and the flavor of butter without the butter scorching. It should shimmer, not smoke.

instructions.title: Cook prosciutto side down
instructions.text: Lay 2 cutlets prosciutto side down in the pan and press them flat with a spatula for the first 20 seconds so the ham makes full contact. Cook 2 1/2 to 3 minutes without moving, until the prosciutto is deep bronze and crisp at the edges. Resist flipping early; that crackly ham surface is the entire dish.

instructions.title: Flip and finish
instructions.text: Turn the cutlets over and cook 2 minutes more on the floured side, until golden. Check the thickest one with an instant-read thermometer and pull only once it reads 165°F (74°C); if it is short, give it another 30 seconds and check again. Move them to a warm plate and cook the second pair the same way, adding the extra 1 tsp oil if the pan looks dry. Prosciutto leaves a lot of rendered fat behind, so you may not need any.

instructions.title: Deglaze the pan
instructions.text: Pour the 1/2 cup white wine into the empty skillet over medium-high heat and scrape up the browned bits with a wooden spoon. Let it bubble down for about 2 minutes, until reduced by half and no longer smelling boozy. There will be a lot of salty, sagey fond in that pan and you want all of it.

instructions.title: Reduce with stock
instructions.text: Add the 1/2 cup chicken stock and simmer 3 minutes until the liquid is reduced to roughly 1/3 cup and looks slightly syrupy. Taste it before adding any salt — prosciutto fond is salty enough that it usually needs none. This is a small, intense sauce, not a pool.

instructions.title: Emulsify and serve
instructions.text: Take the pan off the heat, swirl in the 3 tbsp cold butter piece by piece until glossy, then stir in the 1 tbsp lemon juice. Spoon the sauce around the cutlets rather than over them so the crisp prosciutto stays crisp. Finish with the flaky salt and serve right away, while the ham still crackles.

tips: Ask the deli to slice the prosciutto thin but not paper-thin, and to layer it between parchment. Slices that are too delicate tear when you lift them.
Fresh sage only. Dried sage tastes dusty here and there are no other flavors to hide behind.
Veal scaloppine is the Roman original if you can find it — cook it exactly the same way, about 90 seconds per side.
Assemble the cutlets up to 4 hours ahead, cover, and refrigerate. Let them sit out 15 minutes before cooking so they cook evenly.
recipes.keyTemp: Chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; thin cutlets get there in about 5 minutes total.
recipes.pairing: Sauteed spinach with garlic and a crisp Frascati or Vermentino.

recipes.title: Chicken Cacciatore with Peppers
recipes.blurb: Hunter's chicken — bone-in thighs braised with peppers, onions, wine, and tomatoes until the meat slides off the bone. It is a one-pot dinner that gets better the day after you make it.

items: 8 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (about 3 lb / 1.35 kg)
1 large yellow onion, sliced 1/4 in (6 mm) thick
1 red bell pepper, cut into 1/2 in (12 mm) strips
1 yellow bell pepper, cut into 1/2 in (12 mm) strips
3/4 cup (180 ml) dry red wine, such as Chianti
1 can (28 oz / 794 g) whole peeled tomatoes, crushed by hand
1/3 cup (45 g) pitted Kalamata or Gaeta olives, halved
3 tbsp (12 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley

instructions.title: Dry and season the thighs
instructions.text: Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels, then season all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper. If you have 30 extra minutes, let them sit on a rack in the fridge uncovered — dry skin browns and wet skin steams. Take them out of the fridge about 20 minutes before cooking.

instructions.title: Brown the skin properly
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay in the thighs skin side down, 4 at a time. Cook 6 to 8 minutes without touching them, until the skin is deep golden brown and releases from the pan on its own. If the skin sticks, it is not ready to flip. Brown the second side for 3 minutes, then move all the thighs to a plate.

instructions.title: Pour off excess fat
instructions.text: Spoon off all but about 2 tbsp of the rendered fat, leaving every bit of the browned residue on the bottom of the pot. Chicken thighs give up a surprising amount of fat and leaving it all in makes a greasy braise. That brown layer on the pot is pure flavor and it goes into the sauce in two minutes.

instructions.title: Soften the vegetables
instructions.text: Add the sliced onion and both bell peppers with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until they are limp and just beginning to color at the edges. The salt pulls water out of the vegetables, which loosens the fond so you can scrape it up. Do not rush this into a hard sear; you want them sweet and soft.

instructions.title: Brown the mushrooms
instructions.text: Add the quartered mushrooms and cook 5 minutes more over medium-high, stirring only occasionally so they get some real color. They will release liquid first and then start to brown once it evaporates. Stir in the sliced garlic and the 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 45 seconds until fragrant.

instructions.title: Cook the tomato paste
instructions.text: Push the vegetables to one side, add the 1 tbsp tomato paste to the bare spot, and fry it for 60 to 90 seconds, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick. Cooking the paste this way removes its tinny raw edge and builds a deep savory base. Then stir it through the vegetables.

instructions.title: Deglaze with red wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup red wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard while it bubbles. Simmer 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by half and the sharp alcohol smell is gone. Under-reduced wine leaves the whole braise tasting thin and acidic, so let it cook down properly.

instructions.title: Add tomatoes and herbs
instructions.text: Stir in the hand-crushed tomatoes with their juice, the rosemary and thyme sprigs, and the bay leaf. Bring everything to a gentle simmer. Crushing whole tomatoes by hand gives you a rustic sauce with real texture instead of the uniform slurry you get from a can of crushed.

instructions.title: Nestle the chicken back in
instructions.text: Return the thighs and any juices to the pot skin side up, arranging them so the skin stays above the sauce line. Half-submerged chicken keeps its browned skin instead of turning to wet rubber. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the thighs; add 1/4 cup water if it is much lower.

instructions.title: Braise low and slow
instructions.text: Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer over low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, adjusting so the surface barely blips rather than boils. Thighs are safe at 165°F (74°C) but they are genuinely tender closer to 185°F (85°C), when the connective tissue has melted. A hard boil will tighten the meat, so keep it lazy.

instructions.title: Finish with olives
instructions.text: Fish out the rosemary and thyme stems and the bay leaf, then stir the halved olives into the sauce around the chicken and simmer uncovered for 5 more minutes. Adding olives at the end keeps them bright and firm instead of leaching salt through the whole pot. Taste the sauce and adjust the salt now.

instructions.title: Rest and serve
instructions.text: Let the pot sit off the heat for 10 minutes so the sauce thickens slightly and the chicken reabsorbs its juices. Scatter the 3 tbsp parsley over everything just before serving. Bring it to the table in the pot with plenty of bread — this is a dish that wants to be eaten out of the middle.

tips: Cacciatore is genuinely better on day two. Cool it, refrigerate, and reheat gently on the stove; crisp the skin under the broiler for 2 minutes if you want it back.
Bone-in thighs are non-negotiable for flavor. Boneless thighs work in a pinch but cut the braise to 20 minutes and expect a thinner sauce.
If your sauce is watery at the end, lift out the chicken and boil the sauce hard for 5 minutes to reduce before serving.
A 2 in (5 cm) piece of Parmesan rind dropped in with the tomatoes adds savory depth for free. Remove it before serving.
White wine and no peppers gives you the lighter Tuscan version; both are traditional depending on which part of Italy you ask.
recipes.keyTemp: Thighs are safe at 165°F (74°C) but braise them to about 185°F (85°C) for meat that pulls off the bone.
recipes.pairing: Soft polenta or crusty bread, and a glass of the same Chianti that went into the pot.

recipes.title: Eggplant Parmigiana
recipes.blurb: Layers of silky roasted eggplant, long-simmered tomato, torn basil, and three cheeses that set into clean, tall squares. Made properly it tastes rich without ever being greasy.

items: 1 tbsp kosher salt, for drawing out moisture
2 cans (28 oz / 794 g each) whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes, crushed by hand
1 cup (25 g) fresh basil leaves, divided
16 oz (450 g) low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella, coarsely shredded
1 cup (250 g) whole-milk ricotta, drained 30 minutes if wet

instructions.title: Slice and salt the eggplant
instructions.text: Trim the eggplants and cut them lengthwise into 1/3 in (8 mm) planks — thinner slices collapse into mush and thicker ones stay spongy. Lay them on racks set over sheet pans and sprinkle both sides with the 1 tbsp kosher salt. Let them sweat for 30 minutes, until you see beads of moisture on the surface. Salting pulls out water so the finished dish is not soupy and seasons the eggplant from the inside.

instructions.title: Start the sauce
instructions.text: While the eggplant sweats, warm the 3 tbsp olive oil and sliced garlic in a large saucepan over medium-low for 3 minutes, until the garlic is fragrant and pale gold. Add both cans of hand-crushed tomatoes, 1 tsp salt, and the 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes. Bring to a simmer, then cook uncovered over low heat for 40 to 45 minutes.

instructions.title: Reduce it properly
instructions.text: Stir the sauce every 10 minutes and let it reduce until a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that closes slowly, roughly the texture of loose jam. You should end with about 5 cups. A thin, watery sauce is the single biggest cause of eggplant parm that slumps into a puddle on the plate. Stir in half the basil off the heat.

instructions.title: Dry and oil the slices
instructions.text: Press the eggplant slices firmly between paper towels or a clean kitchen towel to remove the surface water and most of the salt. Brush both sides lightly with the 1/3 cup olive oil — brushing uses a fraction of the oil that frying does, and eggplant will absorb every drop you give it. They should look glossy, not swimming.

instructions.title: Roast until tender
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) and roast the slices on parchment-lined sheet pans for 20 to 25 minutes, flipping once halfway, until they are golden brown and completely floppy. Undercooked eggplant stays rubbery and bitter no matter how long the casserole bakes, so cook it all the way now. Let the slices cool for 10 minutes.

instructions.title: Mix the ricotta
instructions.text: Stir the 1 cup ricotta with the beaten egg and 1/2 cup (50 g) of the Parmigiano until smooth. The egg binds the ricotta so it sets into distinct creamy layers rather than running out when you cut a square. If your ricotta looked watery in the tub, drain it in a sieve for 30 minutes first.

instructions.title: Lower the oven and build
instructions.text: Reduce the oven to 375°F (190°C). Spread 1 cup of sauce across the bottom of a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish so nothing sticks. Lay down a snug single layer of eggplant, slightly overlapping, covering the whole surface. Gaps in the layers are where the finished dish falls apart.

instructions.title: Layer it up
instructions.text: Spread half the ricotta mixture over the eggplant, then a third of the remaining sauce, a third of the mozzarella, and a scattering of Parmigiano and torn basil. Repeat with a second layer of eggplant, the rest of the ricotta, more sauce, and more cheese. Finish with a third layer of eggplant, the last of the sauce, and all the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano on top.

instructions.title: Bake covered
instructions.text: Cover the dish with foil tented so it does not touch the cheese, set it on a rimmed sheet pan to catch drips, and bake for 35 minutes. Covering it first heats everything through gently and lets the layers meld without the top browning too early. You should hear it bubbling when you pull it out.

instructions.title: Uncover and brown
instructions.text: Remove the foil and bake 20 to 25 minutes more, until the top is blistered and deep golden in spots and the sauce is bubbling around the edges. The center should register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer, which tells you the whole casserole is hot through. If the top is pale, run it under the broiler for 90 seconds.

instructions.title: Rest before cutting
instructions.text: Let the dish rest on a rack for at least 25 minutes, and 40 is better. This is not optional — hot eggplant parm is molten and will slide apart the moment a knife touches it, while a rested one cuts into clean squares. Scatter the remaining fresh basil over the top just before serving.

tips: Modern eggplant is bred to be far less bitter, so the salting step is mostly about removing water. Do not skip it anyway — water is the enemy here.
Assemble the whole dish a day ahead, refrigerate unbaked, and add 15 minutes to the covered bake time. It genuinely improves overnight.
Roasting instead of frying uses about a quarter of the oil and makes a dish that is rich rather than heavy. Fried is traditional if you want it.
Fresh mozzarella packed in water will flood the layers. Use the low-moisture block, or tear fresh mozzarella and drain it on towels for an hour first.
Leftovers cut cleanly when cold. Reheat squares at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes rather than microwaving.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake until the center of the casserole reads 165°F (74°C) and the edges bubble; then rest 25 minutes before cutting.
recipes.pairing: A bitter green salad with lemon vinaigrette and a bottle of Aglianico or Nero d'Avola.

recipes.title: Sunday Gravy with Meatballs
recipes.blurb: A big pot of tomato sauce simmered all afternoon with meatballs, sausage, and pork ribs until it turns dark and glossy. Start it after breakfast and let the smell take care of the rest of the day.

items: 1 1/2 cups (75 g) torn day-old white bread, crusts removed
1/3 cup (13 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
3 tbsp (45 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for browning, plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) for finishing the sauce
1 1/2 lb (680 g) bone-in country-style pork ribs
1 lb (450 g) sweet Italian sausage links
3 cans (28 oz / 794 g each) whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes, crushed by hand
2 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste

instructions.title: Make a panade
instructions.text: Tear the bread into small pieces, cover it with the 3/4 cup milk in a bowl, and let it soak 10 minutes until completely soft. Mash it into a paste with a fork. This milk-and-bread paste is called a panade, and it is the reason great meatballs are tender — the starch traps moisture that would otherwise squeeze out as the meat proteins tighten.

instructions.title: Mix the meatballs gently
instructions.text: Add the ground beef, ground pork, beaten eggs, 3/4 cup Parmigiano, minced garlic, parsley, 2 tsp salt, and 1 tsp pepper to the panade. Mix with your hands just until you no longer see streaks of egg, about 30 seconds. Overmixing develops the proteins and gives you meatballs with the texture of a hot dog, so stop early.

instructions.title: Roll and chill
instructions.text: With wet hands, roll the mixture into 16 to 18 balls about 1 3/4 in (4.5 cm) across and 55 g each, roughly the size of a golf ball, setting them on a sheet pan. Wet hands stop the mixture sticking to you. Chill them for 20 minutes if you have time; cold meatballs hold their shape much better when they hit hot oil.

instructions.title: Brown the meatballs
instructions.text: Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the meatballs in two or three batches, about 5 minutes each, turning to get color on several sides. They do not need to be cooked through — they will finish in the sauce for hours. Crowding the pot steams them gray, so give each batch room. Set them aside on a plate.

instructions.title: Brown the pork and sausage
instructions.text: In the same pot, brown the country-style ribs on all sides, about 8 minutes total, then set them aside and brown the sausage links for 5 minutes until well colored. Every one of these browning steps leaves fond on the bottom of the pot, and the layered fond from three different meats is what makes Sunday gravy taste different from ordinary marinara.

instructions.title: Sweat the aromatics
instructions.text: Pour off all but 3 tbsp of fat, then add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat 8 minutes until soft and translucent, scraping the bottom as the onion releases water. Add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 1 minute more. Do not let the garlic brown or the whole pot will carry a bitter edge for hours.

instructions.title: Caramelize the tomato paste
instructions.text: Stir in the 1/4 cup tomato paste and cook it for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens to a deep brick red and starts to stick to the pot. This step concentrates the tomato sugars and drives off the raw canned flavor. It smells noticeably sweeter and rounder when it is ready.

instructions.title: Deglaze with wine
instructions.text: Add the 1 cup red wine and scrape every bit of stuck-on fond loose with a wooden spoon while it bubbles. Simmer 4 to 5 minutes until the wine has reduced by about half and lost its sharp alcohol smell. The pot bottom should be clean and the liquid should look dark and glossy.

instructions.title: Build the pot
instructions.text: Add the three cans of hand-crushed tomatoes, the 2 cups water, 2 tsp salt, and the Parmesan rind, then return the ribs and sausage to the pot. Bring it up to a simmer, then drop the heat until the surface just barely blips once or twice a second. A rolling boil will scorch the bottom and turn the tomatoes bitter.

instructions.title: Simmer, then add the meatballs
instructions.text: Simmer partly covered for 2 hours, stirring every 30 minutes and scraping the bottom each time. Then gently lower the meatballs in, submerging them, and continue to simmer for 1 hour and 15 minutes more. Adding them partway through means they absorb sauce without falling apart over the full cooking time.

instructions.title: Check the meats
instructions.text: The pork ribs are ready when the meat pulls away from the bone with no resistance, around 195°F (91°C) internal, and the sausages should read at least 160°F (71°C). Pull the ribs out, shred the meat off the bones, discard the bones and any cartilage, and stir the meat back in. Slice the sausages into thick coins and return them too.

instructions.title: Finish and season
instructions.text: Fish out the Parmesan rind, then tear the basil leaves in and stir. Taste carefully and adjust with salt — after four hours the sauce is concentrated, so add in small pinches. If it tastes sharp, stir the last 1 tbsp olive oil in off the heat; the fat coats your tongue and rounds the acidity off without making the sauce taste sweet.

instructions.title: Serve in courses
instructions.text: Traditionally the sauce goes on pasta first and the meats come out on a platter afterward as the second course. Spoon a ladle of gravy over each serving and put the platter of meatballs, sausage, and shredded pork in the middle of the table. Give everyone bread; there will be sauce left on every plate.

tips: Sunday gravy freezes beautifully for 3 months. Freeze the sauce and meats together in quart containers, leaving an inch of headroom.
Use 80/20 beef, not lean. Fat is what keeps the meatballs from turning into dry pellets over a long simmer.
If you only have one afternoon and no ribs, the recipe still works with just meatballs and sausage. Cut the initial simmer to 1 hour.
A scorched bottom ruins the whole pot and cannot be fixed. Set a timer to stir every 30 minutes and never let it boil.
Bake the meatballs at 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes instead of frying if you want a cleaner kitchen; you lose a little crust but save a lot of splatter.
recipes.keyTemp: Ground meat is safe at 160°F (71°C), but the ribs want 195°F (91°C) to shred; the meatballs finish far past safe during the long simmer.
recipes.pairing: Rigatoni or a big bowl of ziti, plenty of bread, and a jug of Sangiovese.

recipes.title: Osso Buco alla Milanese
recipes.blurb: Veal shanks braised for three hours until the meat gives way to a spoon, finished with a bright hit of gremolata. The marrow in the center of the bone is the best bite on the plate.

items: 4 cross-cut veal shanks, 1 1/2 in (4 cm) thick (about 3 1/2 lb / 1.6 kg total)
4 ft (1.2 m) kitchen twine, for tying
2 medium carrots, finely diced (about 1 cup / 130 g)
2 celery stalks, finely diced (about 1 cup / 120 g)
2 cups (480 ml) low-sodium veal or chicken stock
1 can (14 oz / 400 g) whole peeled tomatoes, crushed by hand
1/3 cup (13 g) finely chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
2 tsp finely grated lemon zest (from 2 lemons)

instructions.title: Tie the shanks
instructions.text: Wrap a length of kitchen twine around the outside circumference of each shank and tie it snugly, like a belt. Veal shanks are ringed by a band of connective tissue that contracts as it cooks and will pull the whole shank apart into a loose mess. The twine keeps each one in a neat round for three hours. Pat them completely dry afterward.

instructions.title: Season and flour
instructions.text: Season the shanks all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper, then dredge them in the 1/2 cup flour and knock off the excess. The thin flour coat browns quickly and, over the long braise, thickens the sauce to exactly the right body. Only flour them right before they go in the pan, or the coating turns to glue.

instructions.title: Sear hard
instructions.text: Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high until the butter foam subsides. Brown the shanks 5 to 6 minutes per side, in two batches, until they are a deep even brown with no pale patches. This is the most important flavor step in the dish and it cannot be rushed. Set them on a plate; they will look almost cooked, but they are nowhere near done.

instructions.title: Start the soffritto
instructions.text: Lower the heat to medium and add the diced onion, carrot, and celery to the pot with a pinch of salt. Cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is soft and the onion is translucent with just a little golden color. Dice them small and evenly so they melt into the sauce rather than showing up as chunks. Scrape the bottom as the vegetables give up their water.

instructions.title: Add garlic and tomato paste
instructions.text: Stir in the minced garlic and cook 45 seconds, then add the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, stirring, until it darkens to brick red and coats the vegetables. Cooking the paste out removes its raw, tinny taste. The whole pot should smell sweet and deeply savory now.

instructions.title: Deglaze with white wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 1 1/2 cups white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot with a wooden spoon while it bubbles hard. Simmer 5 to 6 minutes until the wine has reduced by roughly half. White wine, not red, is the Milanese tradition — it keeps the sauce light enough that the veal still tastes like veal.

instructions.title: Build the braising liquid
instructions.text: Add the 2 cups stock, the hand-crushed tomatoes, the bay leaves, thyme sprigs, and lemon peel, and bring to a gentle simmer. Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C) while this comes up. Taste the liquid; it should be pleasantly seasoned but not salty, because it will reduce and concentrate over the next three hours.

instructions.title: Return the shanks
instructions.text: Nestle the shanks into the pot in a single layer, standing them so the marrow bones stay upright and the marrow does not slide out. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the meat, not cover it — add a splash of stock if you are short. Spoon a little liquid over the exposed tops.

instructions.title: Braise in the oven
instructions.text: Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the 325°F (165°C) oven for 2 hours and 30 minutes to 3 hours. Check at the 2 hour mark: the liquid should be barely trembling, not bubbling. If it is boiling, drop the oven to 300°F (150°C), since a hard braise squeezes the meat fibers tight and makes veal stringy instead of silky.

instructions.title: Test for doneness
instructions.text: The shanks are ready when a fork slides into the meat with no resistance and the meat has pulled visibly away from the bone, around 200°F (93°C) internal. This is well past any food-safety threshold — collagen only melts into gelatin in that 190°F to 205°F (88°C to 96°C) window. If it is still tight, give it another 30 minutes and check again.

instructions.title: Reduce the sauce
instructions.text: Carefully lift the shanks onto a warm platter and snip off the twine. Fish out the bay leaves, thyme stems, and lemon peel, then simmer the sauce on the stovetop over medium-high for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens enough to coat a spoon. Skim off any orange fat that rises. Taste and adjust the salt.

instructions.title: Make the gremolata
instructions.text: Chop the parsley, lemon zest, and garlic together on a board until they are fine and well mixed, then stir in the flaky salt. Making it at the last minute matters — the volatile oils in raw garlic and lemon zest fade within about 20 minutes. This raw, sharp mixture is what cuts through three hours of richness.

instructions.title: Serve with a marrow spoon
instructions.text: Spoon sauce over each shank, scatter the gremolata generously on top, and set the platter down with small spoons or the handle end of a teaspoon for digging out the marrow. Osso buco means bone with a hole, and that hole is the point. Serve immediately, while everything is hot enough that the marrow is soft.

tips: Ask the butcher for center-cut hind shanks 1 1/2 in (4 cm) thick. Thin shanks dry out and end-cut shanks have almost no marrow.
Osso buco is better made a day ahead. Cool it in its sauce, refrigerate, lift off the solid fat, and reheat at 325°F (165°C) for 40 minutes covered.
Beef shanks are a third of the price and work with the same method, though they need about 30 extra minutes and taste heartier.
Never let the braise boil. If you hear active bubbling through the lid, lower the oven 25 degrees — a trembling surface makes silky meat.
Make the gremolata within 20 minutes of serving. Chopped ahead, it goes dull and slightly bitter.
recipes.keyTemp: Braise to roughly 200°F (93°C) internal — fork-tender, far past the 145°F (63°C) safety point, which is where collagen turns to gelatin.
recipes.pairing: Risotto alla Milanese is the classic partner, with a Barolo or a good Nebbiolo.

recipes.title: Risotto alla Milanese
recipes.blurb: Saffron-gold, loose enough to ripple across the plate, and finished with a shameless amount of butter and Parmigiano. Twenty minutes of stirring buys you the creamiest thing in this book.

items: 1/2 tsp saffron threads (a generous pinch, about 0.4 g)
1 small yellow onion, very finely chopped (about 3/4 cup / 105 g)
1 1/2 cups (300 g) Carnaroli or Arborio rice
1 1/4 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 tbsp (42 g) very cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
1/4 tsp freshly ground white or black pepper
2 tbsp (30 g) beef marrow, finely chopped (optional but traditional)

instructions.title: Bloom the saffron
instructions.text: Bring the 6 cups stock to a bare simmer in a saucepan, then ladle about 1/2 cup of it into a small bowl and crumble the saffron threads into it. Let the saffron steep for at least 10 minutes while you start cooking, until the liquid is a deep orange-red. Blooming pulls the color and flavor out of the threads; tossed in dry, saffron gives you pale, unevenly flavored rice.

instructions.title: Keep the stock hot
instructions.text: Leave the pot of stock on a back burner over low heat, at a temperature where you see steam and the occasional bubble but never a boil. Cold stock added to hot rice shocks the pan, stops the cooking, and adds ten minutes to your risotto. Set a ladle in the pot so it is always in reach.

instructions.title: Sweat the onion
instructions.text: Melt the 1 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a wide heavy saucepan or 4 qt (3.8 L) Dutch oven over medium heat, then add the finely chopped onion and a pinch of salt. Cook 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the onion is completely soft and translucent with no color at all. Browned onion would muddy the clean saffron flavor, so keep the heat gentle.

instructions.title: Toast the rice
instructions.text: Add the 1 1/2 cups rice and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes, until the grains are coated in fat and the edges turn translucent while the centers stay chalky white. This step, called the tostatura, firms the outside of each grain so the risotto stays al dente instead of collapsing into porridge. The rice should smell faintly nutty and click against the spoon.

instructions.title: Add the wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup white wine and stir until it has almost completely evaporated, about 2 minutes. You will hear the sizzle change from a bubbling boil to a drier hiss when it is nearly gone. The wine adds acidity that keeps 4 tablespoons of butter and a cup of cheese from tasting heavy.

instructions.title: Start ladling stock
instructions.text: Add the saffron liquid and one ladle of hot stock, about 3/4 cup, and stir. Keep the heat at a steady medium so the pan is always at a lively simmer — too low and the starch never releases, too high and the outside of the grains blows out before the inside cooks. Stir often but you do not have to stir constantly.

instructions.title: Repeat, ladle by ladle
instructions.text: Each time the liquid reduces enough that dragging the spoon across the pan leaves a clear track for a second, add another ladle of stock and the 1 1/4 tsp salt in stages. Keep going for 16 to 18 minutes total. Adding stock gradually forces the grains to rub against each other, and that friction is what releases the starch that makes risotto creamy.

instructions.title: Taste for al dente
instructions.text: Starting at 16 minutes, bite a grain every couple of minutes. It should be tender all the way through with the faintest firm point at the very center, and absolutely no chalky white core. This usually lands between 17 and 20 minutes depending on your rice. You may not need all the stock, or you may need a splash of hot water.

instructions.title: Get the texture right
instructions.text: The finished risotto should be loose enough that it spreads slowly when you shake the pan — Italians call this all'onda, meaning wavy. If it is stiff, stir in another half ladle of stock. Remember it will tighten noticeably in the next two minutes and again on the plate, so err on the looser side.

instructions.title: Mantecare off the heat
instructions.text: Pull the pan off the burner, wait 30 seconds, then beat in the 3 tbsp cold cubed butter and the 1 cup Parmigiano vigorously with a wooden spoon for a full minute. This is the mantecatura, and beating hard is what emulsifies the fat into the starch and turns the whole pan glossy. Cold butter off the heat emulsifies; warm butter on the heat just makes it greasy. Stir in the marrow now if you are using it.

instructions.title: Rest, then serve at once
instructions.text: Cover the pan and let it sit for 2 minutes, then stir once more and check the salt and the 1/4 tsp pepper. Spoon into warm shallow bowls and tap the bottom of each bowl on the counter so the risotto settles into an even layer. Risotto waits for no one — serve within a minute or two, because it stiffens fast.

tips: Carnaroli holds its shape better than Arborio and is much harder to overcook. If you can find it, buy it; it is the forgiving option.
Never rinse risotto rice. The powdery surface starch is exactly what you are trying to release into the sauce.
Saffron is expensive but you use only a pinch, and the cheap powdered stuff is often adulterated. Buy whole threads from a spice shop.
Leftover risotto spread on a sheet pan and chilled overnight is the starting point for arancini, which is the best reason to make extra.
If you must hold risotto, stop it 3 minutes early, spread it on a cold sheet pan, then finish with hot stock and butter just before serving.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature here — go by the grain: tender through with the barest firm point at the center, and loose enough to ripple when you shake the pan.
recipes.pairing: The traditional partner for osso buco, or eat it alone with a glass of Franciacorta.

recipes.title: Wild Mushroom Risotto
recipes.blurb: Dried porcini soaked into a dark, savory broth, fresh mushrooms browned hard, and rice stirred until it turns to cream. This is the most flavor you can get out of five dollars of dried fungus.

items: 4 cups (960 ml) low-sodium chicken or vegetable stock
12 oz (340 g) mixed fresh mushrooms (cremini, shiitake, oyster), sliced 1/4 in (6 mm)
1 small yellow onion, very finely chopped (about 3/4 cup / 105 g)
1 1/2 cups (300 g) Carnaroli or Arborio rice
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
3 tbsp (42 g) very cold unsalted butter, cubed
2 tbsp (8 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
1 tsp (5 ml) good extra-virgin olive oil, for drizzling

instructions.title: Soak the porcini
instructions.text: Put the 1 oz dried porcini in a heatproof bowl, pour the 2 cups boiling water over them, and press them under with a spoon. Let them soak 20 minutes until fully softened and the water is dark brown. That soaking liquid is the single most valuable ingredient in this recipe, so do not even think about pouring it down the drain.

instructions.title: Strain and combine the broth
instructions.text: Lift the porcini out with a slotted spoon, squeeze them gently over the bowl, and chop them coarsely. Pour the soaking liquid through a coffee filter or a sieve lined with a paper towel to catch the grit that always settles at the bottom. Combine the strained liquid with the 4 cups stock in a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer on a back burner.

instructions.title: Brown the fresh mushrooms
instructions.text: Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp butter in a wide heavy pan over medium-high, add the sliced fresh mushrooms in as close to a single layer as you can, and leave them alone for 4 minutes. They will release water, look wet and gray, then start browning once the liquid cooks off. Continue 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring occasionally, until they are properly dark at the edges.

instructions.title: Season and set aside
instructions.text: Add the 1 tsp thyme and 3/4 tsp salt to the mushrooms and toss for 30 seconds. Season only after browning — salt added at the start draws water out and the mushrooms steam instead of searing. Scrape them onto a plate and reserve about a third for garnishing at the end.

instructions.title: Sweat the onion
instructions.text: In the same pan, melt the 2 tbsp butter over medium heat and cook the finely chopped onion with a pinch of salt for 6 to 7 minutes, until soft and translucent. Scrape the browned mushroom fond off the bottom as the onion releases moisture. Stir in the minced garlic and cook 45 seconds until fragrant.

instructions.title: Toast the rice
instructions.text: Add the 1 1/2 cups rice and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the grains look glossy and the outer edges turn translucent around a white center. You will hear them click against the pan and smell something like toasted popcorn. This toasting keeps the grains distinct instead of dissolving into paste.

instructions.title: Deglaze with wine
instructions.text: Pour in the 3/4 cup white wine and stir until the pan is nearly dry, about 2 minutes, and the sharp smell of alcohol has burned off. The sizzle will go from a wet bubble to a dry hiss when it is ready. Stir in the chopped rehydrated porcini now so they have time to give up their flavor to the rice.

instructions.title: Ladle in the broth
instructions.text: Add a ladle of the hot porcini broth, about 3/4 cup, and stir. Keep the pan at a steady, lively simmer and add another ladle each time the previous one has reduced enough to leave a clear track behind your spoon. Add the 1 tsp salt over the first few additions rather than all at once, since the broth is already savory.

instructions.title: Keep going and taste
instructions.text: Continue the ladle-stir-reduce cycle for 16 to 18 minutes, keeping the rice moving so the grains rub together and release starch. Start tasting at 16 minutes: the grain should be tender through with just a whisper of firmness at the core. If you run out of broth before it is done, use hot water rather than overcooking.

instructions.title: Fold in the mushrooms
instructions.text: Stir in two-thirds of the browned mushrooms and one more small ladle of broth, then cook 1 minute more. The risotto should be loose and wavy, spreading slowly when you shake the pan. Keep it slightly looser than you think you want; it thickens noticeably in the last two minutes.

instructions.title: Mantecare
instructions.text: Take the pan off the heat, wait half a minute, then beat in the 3 tbsp cold cubed butter and the 1 cup Parmigiano hard with a wooden spoon for a full minute. The whole pan should go glossy and creamy as the fat emulsifies into the starch. Season with the 1/2 tsp black pepper and check the salt.

instructions.title: Serve immediately
instructions.text: Spoon into warm shallow bowls, tap each bowl once on the counter so the risotto settles flat, and top with the reserved mushrooms, the chopped parsley, and a thin drizzle of good olive oil. Add a final shower of Parmigiano at the table. Risotto sets up as it cools, so this goes straight from pan to person.

tips: Never skip straining the porcini liquid. There is always sand in the bottom of that bowl and it will end up in every bite.
A splash of dry Marsala or brandy added with the wine deepens the mushroom flavor noticeably for about a dollar.
Use vegetable stock and skip nothing else to make this fully vegetarian; the porcini carry more than enough savoriness.
Cook the mushrooms in two batches if your pan is under 12 in (30 cm). Piled-up mushrooms steam and stay pale and squeaky.
Leftovers make excellent risotto cakes: chill overnight, form 3/4 in (2 cm) patties, and pan-fry in butter for 3 minutes a side.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature — judge by the grain, which should be tender with a faint firm center, and by the risotto rippling slowly when the pan is shaken.
recipes.pairing: A green salad with sharp vinaigrette and a glass of Barbaresco or an earthy Pinot Noir.

recipes.title: Sicilian Arancini Rice Balls
recipes.blurb: Crisp golden spheres of saffron risotto hiding a molten center of ragu, peas, and mozzarella. They are a whole afternoon project and worth every minute of it.

items: 1 small yellow onion, finely chopped (about 3/4 cup / 105 g)
1 small onion, finely chopped (about 1/2 cup / 70 g)
1 cup (240 ml) tomato passata or crushed tomatoes
4 oz (115 g) low-moisture mozzarella, cut into 12 cubes
3 large eggs, beaten with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water
8 cups (2 L) neutral oil, for deep frying
1 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Make the saffron rice
instructions.text: Heat the 6 cups stock to a bare simmer and steep the saffron in a ladleful for 10 minutes. Melt the 3 tbsp butter in a wide pan, soften the chopped onion for 6 minutes, add the 2 cups Arborio and toast 2 minutes, then add the 1/2 cup wine and let it cook away. Ladle in the hot stock and saffron liquid a cup at a time, stirring, for 16 to 18 minutes until the rice is just tender. Two cups of rice drinks roughly three times its volume in liquid, so expect to use most but not quite all of the pot.

instructions.title: Make it stiffer than risotto
instructions.text: Cook this rice until it is noticeably drier than a risotto you would eat with a spoon — it should hold a mound rather than spread. Stir in the 1 1/2 tsp salt and the 1 cup Parmigiano off the heat. Loose rice will not hold a ball shape and the arancini will burst in the fryer, so err firm.

instructions.title: Cool and bind the rice
instructions.text: Spread the rice in a thin layer on a sheet pan and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight, until completely cold and firm. Once cold, mix in the 2 beaten eggs thoroughly with your hands. The egg is the glue that keeps the shell together in hot oil, and it must go into cold rice or it will scramble.

instructions.title: Build the ragu
instructions.text: Heat the 1 tbsp olive oil and brown the 8 oz ground beef over medium-high for 6 minutes, breaking it into small crumbles, then add the chopped onion and cook 5 minutes more. Stir in the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens to brick red. Deglaze with the 1/2 cup red wine and simmer until nearly dry.

instructions.title: Finish the filling
instructions.text: Add the 1 cup passata and 1 tsp salt and simmer over low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, until the mixture is thick enough that a spoon leaves a clean channel through it. Stir in the thawed peas in the last 2 minutes. Chill the ragu completely before filling — warm, loose filling turns your rice ball into a steam bomb.

instructions.title: Shape the arancini
instructions.text: With damp hands, scoop about 1/2 cup (115 g) of cold rice and flatten it into a disc in your palm about 5 in (13 cm) across. Press a shallow well into the center, keeping the rice an even 1/2 in (12 mm) thick all the way around so there are no thin spots to blow out in the oil. Keep a bowl of water nearby and re-wet your hands constantly, because dry hands will tear the rice. The batch should give you 12 discs with a little rice held back for patching.

instructions.title: Fill and seal
instructions.text: Spoon a generous 1 1/2 tbsp (about 30 g) of cold ragu into the well — that is the whole batch divided twelve ways — and press a cube of mozzarella into the middle of it. Fold the edges of the rice up and over the filling, then roll gently between your palms into a smooth ball or the traditional cone shape. Check carefully for cracks and patch them with a little extra rice — a single gap will leak cheese into the oil.

instructions.title: Chill the shaped balls
instructions.text: Set the finished arancini on a parchment-lined sheet pan and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Cold, firm balls hold together in the fryer and heat through more evenly. This is also the natural stopping point if you want to break the project across two days.

instructions.title: Set up the breading
instructions.text: Put the flour in one shallow dish, the 3 eggs beaten with 2 tbsp water in a second, and the breadcrumbs in a third. Roll each ball in flour, then egg, then press it firmly into the breadcrumbs, making sure every square inch is covered. Any bare spot is where the arancino will split open in the oil.

instructions.title: Heat the oil to 350°F
instructions.text: Pour the 8 cups oil into a heavy 4 qt (3.8 L) pot so it stands about 2 1/2 in (6 cm) deep and still comes no more than halfway up the sides, then heat it to 350°F (175°C) on a thermometer. Temperature control matters enormously here: below 325°F (163°C) they go greasy, and above 375°F (190°C) the crust burns before the center is hot. Have a slotted spider and a wire rack ready.

instructions.title: Fry in small batches
instructions.text: Lower 3 or 4 arancini into the oil with a spider and fry 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until they are a deep even golden brown. Let the oil come back to 350°F (175°C) between batches; adding too many at once drops the temperature fast. Check one from the first batch with a thin probe: the center must reach 165°F (74°C), because the ball goes into the oil refrigerator-cold and the ragu inside is cooked ground beef being reheated. If the crust is dark but the center is short of temperature, finish the batch on a rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 minutes.

instructions.title: Drain and rest
instructions.text: Lift them onto a wire rack, never paper towels, and sprinkle immediately with the flaky sea salt while the surface is still oily enough to hold it. Let them rest 5 minutes before biting in; the mozzarella inside is well over 200°F (93°C) and will burn your mouth badly. Serve warm, with extra tomato sauce for dipping if you like.

tips: This is a two-day recipe by design. Make the rice and ragu on day one, shape and fry on day two, and it stops being intimidating.
Leftover Risotto alla Milanese from this chapter is the ideal starting rice. Chill it overnight and skip straight to the egg-binding step.
Fine dry breadcrumbs, not panko, give the smooth crackly shell that arancini are supposed to have.
Shaped, breaded arancini freeze well for 2 months. Fry from frozen at 325°F (163°C) for 7 to 8 minutes so the center catches up.
If one bursts in the oil, take the whole batch out, strain the oil, and check the rest for cracks before continuing.
recipes.keyTemp: Fry at 350°F (175°C) until the center reads 165°F (74°C); the filling contains cooked ground beef, which is safe at 160°F (71°C).
recipes.pairing: Cold beer or a chilled glass of Grillo, with a bowl of marinara for dipping.

recipes.title: Neapolitan Pizza Margherita
recipes.blurb: A slow-fermented dough with a puffed, blistered rim, crushed San Marzano, torn mozzarella, and basil. Two days of waiting and ninety seconds of cooking, and it is the best pizza you will make at home.

items: 500 g (about 4 cups) Italian 00 flour or bread flour
325 g (1 1/3 cups plus 1 tbsp / 325 ml) cool water, 65 percent hydration
Semolina flour, about 1/2 cup (85 g), for dusting the peel
1 can (28 oz / 794 g) whole peeled San Marzano tomatoes
12 oz (340 g) fresh mozzarella di bufala or fior di latte, torn and drained
6 tbsp (90 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, 1 tbsp per pizza before baking and 1/2 tbsp after

instructions.title: Dissolve salt and yeast
instructions.text: Put the 325 g cool water in a large bowl and whisk in the 15 g salt until it dissolves, then whisk in the 1 g yeast. Neapolitan method dissolves the salt in the water first, so it never sits directly against the yeast in a concentrated pocket. Yes, that is a truly tiny amount of yeast — the long cold ferment does the work instead.

instructions.title: Mix a shaggy dough
instructions.text: Add the 500 g flour a third at a time, mixing with your hand or a wooden spoon until there is no dry flour left and you have a rough, sticky mass. Do not knead yet. Cover the bowl and let it rest 20 minutes, which lets the flour fully hydrate and makes the kneading dramatically easier.

instructions.title: Knead until smooth
instructions.text: Turn the dough onto an unfloured counter and knead for 10 to 12 minutes, using a bench scraper to fold it over on itself whenever it sticks. It will go from ragged and tacky to smooth and slightly springy. Test it by stretching a piece thin enough to see light through without tearing — that is the windowpane, and it means the gluten is developed.

instructions.title: Bulk ferment at room temperature
instructions.text: Shape the dough into a tight ball, put it in a lightly oiled container, cover, and leave at room temperature, around 70°F (21°C), for 2 hours. It will not double; you are just waking the yeast up. If your kitchen is much warmer than that, cut this to 90 minutes.

instructions.title: Cold ferment overnight
instructions.text: Move the covered container to the refrigerator for 20 to 24 hours. This slow cold fermentation is where all the flavor comes from — the dough develops complex, faintly sweet, slightly tangy notes that a same-day dough simply cannot have. It will rise slowly and look a little bubbly when you take it out.

instructions.title: Divide and ball
instructions.text: Turn the cold dough out and divide it into 4 equal pieces of about 210 g each, using a scale if you have one. Shape each into a tight ball by folding the edges into the center and then rolling it seam-side down under a cupped hand until the surface is taut. A tight skin is what makes the rim puff dramatically.

instructions.title: Final proof
instructions.text: Set the balls well apart in a covered container or on a floured tray under plastic and let them proof at room temperature for 4 to 6 hours, until they have visibly relaxed, spread slightly, and feel soft and pillowy when poked. An underproofed ball fights back when you stretch it and will not open properly. A gentle poke should leave a dent that fills in slowly.

instructions.title: Preheat as hot as you can
instructions.text: Put a pizza steel or stone on a rack about 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler and heat the oven to its maximum, usually 550°F (290°C), for a full hour. A steel or stone that has only been in for 20 minutes is not saturated with heat and will give you a pale, cracker-like base. Switch the broiler on 10 minutes before the first pizza goes in.

instructions.title: Make the sauce
instructions.text: Crush the canned tomatoes by hand or pass them through a food mill, then stir in the 1 1/2 tsp salt. Do not cook it and do not add garlic or herbs — the sauce cooks in 90 seconds on the pizza and stays bright and fresh that way. If it looks watery, drain off some of the thin juice.

instructions.title: Open the dough by hand
instructions.text: Flour a work surface, lay a ball down, and press from the center outward with your fingertips, leaving the outer 3/4 in (2 cm) completely untouched. Then lift the disc and let gravity stretch it as you rotate it over your knuckles until it is about 10 in (25 cm) across. Never use a rolling pin — it crushes the gas out of the rim and you lose the cornicione entirely.

instructions.title: Top fast and lightly
instructions.text: Slide the disc onto a semolina-dusted peel, spread about 1/3 cup of sauce in a spiral leaving the rim bare, scatter a quarter of the torn mozzarella, and drizzle with 1 tbsp of the olive oil. If you are using the Parmigiano, dust about 1 tbsp of it over the sauce before the mozzarella goes on — it is not strictly Neapolitan, but it adds a savory backbone in a home oven that cannot reach wood-fired heat. Work in under 60 seconds; dough sitting on a peel starts to stick almost immediately. Shake the peel gently to confirm it slides before you go anywhere near the oven.

instructions.title: Bake under the broiler
instructions.text: Slide the pizza onto the hot steel with a quick forward-and-back jerk and bake under the broiler for 4 to 6 minutes, until the rim is puffed with dark leopard spots and the cheese is bubbling. Turn the pizza halfway through with the peel for even color. Home ovens run cooler than a wood oven, so watch for color rather than the clock.

instructions.title: Finish with basil
instructions.text: Pull the pizza out, add 6 fresh basil leaves, and drizzle with another 1/2 tbsp of the olive oil. Basil added before baking turns black and bitter, which is why real pizzerias tuck it under the cheese or add it after. Cut and eat immediately, standing up, before making the next one.

tips: Weigh everything. Pizza dough is a percentage formula and cup measurements can be off by 15 percent, which is the difference between good and unworkable.
A baking steel outperforms a stone by a wide margin because it transfers heat faster, which is exactly what a home oven lacks.
The dough can hold in the fridge for up to 72 hours and gets more flavorful every day. Just pull it 5 to 6 hours before you want to bake.
Drain torn fresh mozzarella on paper towels for 20 minutes. Undrained buffalo mozzarella will flood the center of the pizza.
If the dough springs back and refuses to open, cover it and wait 15 minutes. Fighting it only tears it.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at the oven's maximum, ideally 550°F (290°C) with the broiler on, until the rim is puffed and leopard-spotted, 4 to 6 minutes.
recipes.pairing: Cold Peroni or a light Aglianico, and nothing else on the table.

recipes.title: Sicilian Pan Pizza
recipes.blurb: A thick, airy square with a fried-crisp bottom, cheese caramelized right into the edge of the pan, and sauce spooned over the top. Far more forgiving than round pizza and arguably more fun to eat.

items: 300 g (1 1/4 cups / 300 ml) lukewarm water, 75 percent hydration
2 tbsp (30 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the dough
3 tbsp (45 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the pan
10 oz (285 g) low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella, cut into 1/2 in (12 mm) cubes
2 oz (55 g) sharp provolone or aged white cheddar, shredded

instructions.title: Mix a wet dough
instructions.text: Stir the 400 g bread flour, 300 g lukewarm water, 9 g salt, and 3 g instant yeast together in a bowl with a spoon or your hand until no dry flour remains, about 1 minute. Add the 2 tbsp olive oil and squish it in. The dough will be very wet and sticky and that is correct — 75 percent hydration is what gives you the open, airy crumb.

instructions.title: Rest, then fold
instructions.text: Cover the bowl and let it sit 20 minutes, then do a set of stretch and folds: wet your hand, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up, and fold it over the center, rotating the bowl and repeating four times. Do three sets of folds spaced 20 minutes apart. Folding builds strength in a wet dough without any kneading.

instructions.title: Bulk ferment
instructions.text: Cover the bowl and leave it at room temperature, about 70°F (21°C), for 1 1/2 to 2 hours more — roughly 3 hours from mixing once you count the hour of folds — until the dough has doubled and the surface is dotted with bubbles. If your kitchen is cold this can take an hour longer, so judge by the look and not the clock. The dough should feel alive and jiggly when you shake the bowl.

instructions.title: Oil the pan generously
instructions.text: Pour the 3 tbsp olive oil into a 13x9 in (33x23 cm) metal baking pan or a quarter sheet pan and spread it up the sides with your fingers. That much oil sounds like a lot but it is the whole point — the dough essentially shallow-fries against the pan and comes out with a crisp, golden bottom crust.

instructions.title: Transfer and let it relax
instructions.text: Scrape the dough into the oiled pan, turn it once to coat both sides, and press it toward the corners with oiled fingertips. It will spring back and refuse to reach the edges, which is normal. Cover and wait 20 minutes, then press again; the gluten relaxes and it will go the rest of the way easily.

instructions.title: Second proof in the pan
instructions.text: Cover the pan loosely and let the dough proof for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, until it is visibly puffy, has filled the corners, and a light poke leaves a dent that springs back only halfway. Underproofed dough bakes dense and bready. This is the stage that decides whether your crumb is open or tight.

instructions.title: Make the sauce
instructions.text: While it proofs, warm the 2 tbsp olive oil with the minced garlic over medium-low for 2 minutes until fragrant but not colored. Add the crushed tomatoes, 1 tsp oregano, 3/4 tsp salt, red pepper flakes, and 1 tsp sugar, and simmer 20 minutes until thickened. Sicilian style spoons the sauce on top of the cheese, so it needs to be thick enough not to run.

instructions.title: Preheat with a stone
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 500°F (260°C) with a baking steel or stone on the lowest rack for at least 45 minutes. Setting the pan directly on preheated steel blasts the bottom crust with heat and is the difference between crisp and pale. If you have neither, use the lowest oven rack.

instructions.title: Dimple and top
instructions.text: Press your oiled fingertips into the proofed dough all over, going nearly to the bottom of the pan, to create dimples. Scatter the cubed mozzarella and shredded provolone evenly across the surface, pushing some cubes right up against the edges of the pan. Those edge cubes melt down the sides and fry into the caramelized cheese crust that makes this style famous.

instructions.title: Add the sauce in stripes
instructions.text: Spoon the sauce over the cheese in three or four thick stripes rather than spreading it everywhere. Leaving cheese exposed lets it brown and bubble, and stripes are the traditional look. Use about 1 1/2 cups of sauce and save the rest for dipping.

instructions.title: Bake until deeply browned
instructions.text: Set the pan on the hot steel and bake 18 to 22 minutes, until the cheese at the edges is dark brown and crackling and the top is bubbling. At 500°F (260°C) that is genuinely enough to cook a pan this thick through — push it to 25 minutes and the cheese crust crosses from caramelized into acrid. Do not pull it at the first sign of golden either; this style wants real color. Lift a corner with a spatula to check that the bottom is crisp and browned before you commit.

instructions.title: Release and rest
instructions.text: Run a thin metal spatula around the edges immediately to free the cheese crust, then slide the whole pizza out onto a wire rack within 2 minutes. Leaving it in the pan traps steam and softens that bottom crust you just worked for. Rest 5 minutes, scatter the Pecorino and basil, and cut into 8 squares.

tips: A dark metal or steel pan browns the bottom far better than glass or ceramic. Cast iron works beautifully too.
The dough can bulk ferment in the refrigerator overnight instead. Bring it to room temperature for 2 hours before pressing it into the pan.
Pepperoni cups nicely on this style; add it under the sauce stripes so the edges curl and crisp without burning.
If the dough tears while you press it, stop and let it rest 15 more minutes. Torn gluten will not proof evenly.
Leftovers reheat perfectly in a dry skillet over medium heat for 4 minutes with a lid on, which re-crisps the base.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 500°F (260°C) for 18 to 22 minutes until the cheese edges are deep brown and the bottom crust is crisp and golden.
recipes.pairing: Cold lager and a big bowl of dressed greens to cut the richness.
