recipes.title: Rosemary Sea Salt Focaccia
recipes.blurb: A dimpled, olive-oil-soaked slab with a crackly bottom and a cloud-soft middle. It takes about fifteen minutes of actual work and makes the whole apartment smell incredible.

items: 400 g (1 2/3 cups / 400 ml) lukewarm water, about 100°F (38°C)
3 tbsp (45 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the dough
4 tbsp (60 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the pan
2 tbsp (30 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for the top
2 tbsp (4 g) fresh rosemary leaves, roughly chopped

instructions.title: Wake up the yeast
instructions.text: Whisk the 5 g instant yeast and 1 tsp honey into the 400 g lukewarm water and let it sit 5 minutes until it looks slightly cloudy and smells faintly of bread. The water should feel like a warm bath, around 100°F (38°C) — anything above 120°F (49°C) starts killing yeast. Instant yeast does not strictly need proofing, but this tells you it is alive before you commit.

instructions.title: Mix by hand
instructions.text: Add the 500 g bread flour and 10 g fine sea salt to the water and stir with a sturdy spoon or your hand for about 90 seconds, until there are no dry patches and you have a shaggy, very wet dough. Then drizzle in the 3 tbsp olive oil and squish it through. There is no kneading in this recipe at all — time does the work.

instructions.title: Do two sets of folds
instructions.text: Cover the bowl and rest 30 minutes, then wet your hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it upward, and fold it over the middle; rotate the bowl and repeat four times. Rest 30 minutes and do one more set. These folds build the gluten structure that traps the big bubbles you want in focaccia.

instructions.title: Bulk ferment until doubled
instructions.text: Cover the bowl tightly and leave it at room temperature for 2 more hours, which puts you at about 3 hours of fermentation counting the hour you spent folding, until the dough has doubled in size and is full of visible bubbles across the surface. In a cool kitchen this may take an hour longer, so watch the dough and not the clock. It should look inflated and wobble when you nudge the bowl.

instructions.title: Oil the pan properly
instructions.text: Pour the 4 tbsp olive oil into a 13x9 in (33x23 cm) metal pan or a quarter sheet pan and use your fingers to coat the bottom and all four sides thoroughly. This is more oil than feels reasonable and it is doing something specific: the underside of the focaccia essentially fries in it and comes out golden and crisp.

instructions.title: Transfer without deflating
instructions.text: Slide an oiled hand or bowl scraper down the side of the bowl and gently ease the whole mass of dough into the pan in one piece. Handle it as if it were a sleeping cat — every big bubble you knock out is a hole you will not have in the finished bread. Turn it once so both sides are oiled.

instructions.title: Coax it to the corners
instructions.text: Press the dough outward toward the corners with flat, oiled fingers. It will pull back and stop short of the edges the first time, which is normal. Wait 15 minutes and press again, and by the second or third try it will reach all four corners with no fighting.

instructions.title: Proof in the pan
instructions.text: Cover the pan loosely and let the dough proof 45 minutes to 1 hour, until it is puffy and jiggly and has risen visibly up the sides. Poke it gently: the dent should fill back in slowly and only partway. Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) about 30 minutes into this proof.

instructions.title: Dimple with authority
instructions.text: Drizzle the 2 tbsp of top olive oil over the surface, then press all ten fingertips straight down through the dough until you feel the pan bottom, working across the whole surface. Do not be gentle — real dimples are what hold the pools of oil that define focaccia. The dough will deflate slightly and then recover in the oven.

instructions.title: Season the top
instructions.text: Scatter the 2 tbsp chopped rosemary, 1 1/2 tsp flaky salt, and 1/4 tsp cracked pepper evenly across the surface, pushing a little rosemary into the dimples so it does not scorch. Rosemary sitting fully exposed on top of a 450°F (230°C) bake will blacken. Let the pan sit 10 more minutes while the oven finishes heating.

instructions.title: Bake until deep gold
instructions.text: Bake on a lower-middle rack for 22 to 27 minutes, rotating the pan halfway, until the top is deeply golden and the edges are dark and crisp. The internal temperature of a fully baked focaccia is 200°F to 205°F (93°C to 96°C) if you want to check. Pale focaccia tastes doughy, so push it further than you think.

instructions.title: Get it out of the pan
instructions.text: Run a spatula around the edges and slide the focaccia onto a wire rack within 2 minutes of leaving the oven. Steam trapped under the bread in a hot pan will turn that crisp bottom soggy in about five minutes. Cool at least 15 minutes before cutting into 12 squares.

tips: For much better flavor, do the bulk ferment in the fridge overnight, up to 24 hours. Bring the dough to room temperature for an hour before panning it.
Halved cherry tomatoes, thin lemon slices, or olives pressed into the dimples before baking all work; press them in deep so they do not burn.
If your dough will not reach the corners, you are being too impatient. Rest 15 minutes and try again rather than forcing and tearing it.
Weigh the flour if you possibly can. A cup of flour can vary by 20 g depending on how you scoop, and this dough is sensitive to it.
Focaccia is best the day it is baked. Day-two slices come back to life in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 5 minutes, or split them for sandwiches.
recipes.keyTemp: Bake at 450°F (230°C) until deep golden; the center of a finished loaf reads 200°F to 205°F (93°C to 96°C).
recipes.pairing: Good olive oil and balsamic for dipping, a plate of prosciutto, and a glass of something cold.

recipes.title: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
recipes.blurb: Thick bread grilled until it is charred at the edges, rubbed with raw garlic, and piled with tomatoes that have been salted just long enough to taste like summer. Five ingredients, and every one of them has to be good.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) ripe tomatoes, preferably a mix of heirloom and cherry
1/2 cup (12 g) fresh basil leaves, torn
3 tbsp (45 ml) good extra-virgin olive oil, plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) for drizzling at the end
8 slices country sourdough or ciabatta, 3/4 in (2 cm) thick
3 tbsp (45 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, for brushing
2 large garlic cloves, peeled and halved
1/2 tsp flaky sea salt, for finishing

instructions.title: Choose good tomatoes
instructions.text: Use tomatoes that smell like tomatoes at the stem end and give slightly when you press them. Pale, hard, refrigerated supermarket tomatoes in February will make a sad bruschetta no matter how good your technique is. If good tomatoes are not available, use cherry or grape tomatoes, which are reliable year round.

instructions.title: Cut and salt them
instructions.text: Core the large tomatoes and cut them into 1/2 in (12 mm) dice, halve any cherry tomatoes, and put everything in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the 3/4 tsp kosher salt and let them drain for 15 to 20 minutes. Salting draws out the watery juice that would otherwise turn your toast to mush, and it seasons the tomatoes all the way through.

instructions.title: Save the tomato water
instructions.text: You will end up with about 1/3 cup of pink tomato liquid in the bowl below. Do not throw it away — it is intensely flavorful. Either sip it, add it to a vinaigrette, or reduce it in a small pan for two minutes and spoon it over the finished bruschetta.

instructions.title: Dress the tomatoes
instructions.text: Move the drained tomatoes to a clean bowl and toss with the 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp red wine vinegar, torn basil, and 1/4 tsp black pepper. Tear the basil with your hands rather than chopping it, since a knife bruises the leaves and turns the cut edges black. Let it sit at room temperature while you toast the bread.

instructions.title: Cut the bread thick
instructions.text: Slice the loaf into 8 pieces about 3/4 in (2 cm) thick, cutting on a slight angle if the loaf is narrow so you get more surface area. Thin slices go limp under wet tomatoes within a minute. You want slices sturdy enough to pick up with one hand.

instructions.title: Brush with oil
instructions.text: Brush both sides of each slice lightly with the 3 tbsp olive oil, using about half a teaspoon per side. The oil helps the surface toast rather than dry out, and it carries flavor into the crumb. Do not soak the bread; it should look lightly sheened, not saturated.

instructions.title: Grill or broil the bread
instructions.text: Cook the slices on a hot grill, in a ridged grill pan over medium-high, or under the broiler 6 in (15 cm) from the element. Give them 2 to 3 minutes per side, until you have dark char marks on the ridges and a crisp, dry surface. Bruschetta gets its name from bruscare, meaning to char, so a little real blackening is authentic and delicious.

instructions.title: Rub with raw garlic
instructions.text: While each slice is still hot, drag a cut half of garlic clove firmly across the rough, toasted surface. The bread acts like a grater and the garlic melts into it. One clove half will do about four slices; go lighter if you are garlic-shy, because raw garlic on hot bread is potent.

instructions.title: Top just before serving
instructions.text: Spoon the dressed tomatoes generously onto each slice, letting a little juice soak in but not pooling. Do this within a minute or two of eating — bruschetta assembled ahead of time becomes soggy bread with a salad on it. Set the toasts out and top them at the table if you are feeding a crowd.

instructions.title: Finish and eat
instructions.text: Drizzle the last 1 tbsp of good olive oil over the toasts, sprinkle the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt on top, and add a few whole basil leaves for looks. Serve immediately, with a plate underneath because the juice will run. This is a dish that rewards eating standing in the kitchen.

tips: The salting and draining step is what separates real bruschetta from soggy toast. Do not skip it even if the tomatoes look dry.
Day-old bread is better than fresh here; it toasts drier and holds up longer under the topping.
Use your best olive oil for the topping, since it is never heated and you taste it directly. Save the ordinary bottle for brushing the bread.
The tomato mixture can be made up to 2 hours ahead and left at room temperature. Never refrigerate it, which kills tomato flavor and turns the texture mealy.
A spoonful of the topping over burrata or grilled fish is a very good use of leftovers.
recipes.keyTemp: No internal temperature — toast the bread until the surface is dry, crisp, and charred in spots on the ridges, about 2 to 3 minutes per side.
recipes.pairing: A chilled glass of Vermentino or Prosecco, as the first thing you put on the table.

recipes.title: Caprese Salad with Torn Basil
recipes.blurb: Tomato, mozzarella, basil, olive oil, salt — the whole dish is in choosing well and seasoning properly. When the tomatoes are right, nothing on the table beats it.

items: 1 1/2 lb (680 g) ripe tomatoes (about 3 large), at room temperature
12 oz (340 g) fresh mozzarella di bufala or fior di latte
1/4 cup (60 ml) best-quality extra-virgin olive oil
1 tsp flaky sea salt, such as Maldon

instructions.title: Bring everything to room temperature
instructions.text: Take the tomatoes and mozzarella out of the refrigerator at least 30 minutes before you plan to eat, and an hour is better. Cold mutes flavor and firms up the fat in cheese, so a fridge-cold caprese tastes like almost nothing. Never store tomatoes in the fridge in the first place, since below 55°F (13°C) they lose their aroma permanently.

instructions.title: Choose your tomatoes
instructions.text: Look for tomatoes that feel heavy for their size, smell green and sweet at the stem, and yield slightly to a gentle squeeze. A mix of colors — red, yellow, and a dark heirloom — looks beautiful, but flavor beats color every time. If it is winter, use ripe cherry tomatoes instead and halve them.

instructions.title: Drain the mozzarella
instructions.text: Lift the mozzarella out of its liquid and set it on a double layer of paper towels for 10 minutes, turning once. Fresh mozzarella carries a lot of water, and undrained cheese will release a milky pool that dilutes the olive oil into a watery mess. Save the liquid to store any leftover cheese.

instructions.title: Slice the tomatoes
instructions.text: Core the tomatoes and cut them into slices about 1/3 in (8 mm) thick with a very sharp or serrated knife, using a gentle sawing motion so you do not crush them. Cut through the equator rather than pole to pole for the prettiest cross sections. Lay them on a plate as you go.

instructions.title: Salt the tomatoes first
instructions.text: Sprinkle the tomato slices with about half of the flaky salt and let them sit for 5 minutes. This small head start seasons the tomatoes properly and pulls a little juice to the surface, which then mixes with the olive oil into an instant dressing. Salting everything at the end leaves the tomato itself tasting flat.

instructions.title: Slice the mozzarella
instructions.text: Cut the drained mozzarella into slices roughly the same 1/3 in (8 mm) thickness as the tomatoes so every bite is balanced. Wipe the knife between cuts if the cheese drags. For buffalo mozzarella, tearing it into rough pieces by hand is more traditional and gives the oil more nooks to sit in.

instructions.title: Arrange the plate
instructions.text: Overlap the tomato and mozzarella slices in alternating rows or a spiral on a large platter, or simply pile them casually — both are correct. Do not build a tall tower; caprese should be shallow so the oil and juices pool where you can get at them with bread. Work on a flat platter rather than a bowl.

instructions.title: Tear the basil
instructions.text: Tear the basil leaves in half by hand and tuck them between the layers as well as scattering some on top. Torn basil releases its oils without the bruising and blackening you get from a knife blade. Add it at the very last moment, because basil wilts and darkens within a few minutes of being dressed.

instructions.title: Dress and finish
instructions.text: Drizzle the 1/4 cup olive oil over everything in a slow, generous stream, then finish with the remaining flaky salt and the 1/2 tsp cracked pepper. If you are using it, add only a few drops of aged balsamic — the thick sweet syrup, not the thin sharp supermarket kind, and never enough to hide the tomato. Serve within 10 minutes, with bread for the plate.

tips: This dish has nowhere to hide. Buy the best tomatoes, the best mozzarella, and the best olive oil you can, and make something else in January.
Buffalo mozzarella is creamier and tangier; fior di latte is milder and firmer and slices more cleanly. Both are correct.
Skip the balsamic entirely if your tomatoes are excellent. In Italy caprese usually gets nothing but oil and salt.
Burrata instead of mozzarella turns this into a richer dish; tear it open at the table so the cream runs into the tomato juices.
Assemble at the last minute. A caprese that has sat for 30 minutes is a puddle with cheese in it.
recipes.keyTemp: No cooking involved — serve everything at room temperature, around 68°F to 72°F (20°C to 22°C), which is when tomatoes and mozzarella taste their best.
recipes.pairing: Crusty bread for mopping the plate and a cold glass of Falanghina or a dry rosato.
